title: Six loop challenges
idea: An accumulator is a variable that a loop updates on every pass, turning many items into one result.

analogy.text: A cashier's running total. The till starts at zero, each scanned item adds to it, and the receipt prints once the last item is scanned.
analogy.breaks: A till only adds; an accumulator can also multiply, join or compare.

points: The start value is also the answer when the loop makes zero passes.
Each pass combines the variable's old value with one new item.
Choose the loop by what you have: a count, a collection or a condition.
A failing test shows what you returned; trace its input by hand.

challenges.intro: Write each function, run the tests, and open a hint only when you are stuck.

items.title: Sum 1 to n
items.prompt: Write `sumTo(n)`. Return 1 + 2 + ... + n. For `n` below 1, return `0`. For example, `sumTo(4)` is 10.
hints: Count from 1 up to `n` with a `for` loop, and keep a running total in a variable declared before the loop.
Start `total` at `0`. Write the test as `i <= n`, so that `n` itself is added.
`for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) { total += i; }`, then `return total`. For `n` below 1 the loop never runs.

items.title: Count down
items.prompt: Write `countdown(n)` using a `while` loop. Return an array from `n` down to 1, such as `[3, 2, 1]`. For `n` below 1, return `[]`.
hints: A `while` loop repeats as long as its test is true. Here the test is that `n` is at least 1.
Push `n` onto an array, then lower `n` by 1 inside the loop body.
`while (n >= 1) { out.push(n); n--; }`, then `return out`. Without `n--` the loop never ends.

items.title: Factorial
items.prompt: Write `factorial(n)`. Return 1 * 2 * ... * n. `n` is a whole number, 0 or more, and `factorial(0)` is `1`.
hints: Many numbers become one product, so you need an accumulator. Which start value leaves a product unchanged?
A product starts at `1`, because anything times 0 is 0. Loop `i` from 2 up to `n` and multiply: `result *= i`.
`let result = 1; for (let i = 2; i <= n; i++) { result *= i; }`, then `return result`.

items.title: Count the vowels
items.prompt: Write `countVowels(text)`. Return how many of the letters `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u` appear in `text`, in upper or lower case. `y` does not count.
hints: `for (const letter of text)` walks a string one character at a time.
Compare in one case: `text.toLowerCase()` returns the text in lower case, so you only check five letters.
Inside the loop, `if ('aeiou'.includes(letter)) { count++; }`. Return `count` after the loop.

items.title: Reverse a string
items.prompt: Write `reverseText(text)`. Return the characters of `text` in reverse order, built with a loop. For example, `'abc'` becomes `'cba'`.
hints: Build a new string, one character per pass, starting from an empty string `''`.
Adding each character to the end copies the order. Add each new character to the front instead.
`result = ch + result;` inside `for (const ch of text)`. Then `return result`.

items.title: Find the largest
items.prompt: Write `largest(numbers)`. Return the biggest number in the array. The numbers may be negative. For an empty array, return `undefined`.
hints: Keep the biggest number seen so far in a variable, and compare every item with it.
Do not start at `0`: if every number is negative, `0` would win. Start from the first item.
`let best = numbers[0];`, then in the loop `if (n > best) { best = n; }`. Return `best`.

pitfalls: Declare the accumulator before the loop; inside the body it resets every pass.
Use `i <= n` when `n` itself counts; `i < n` stops one pass early.
A `return` inside the loop body ends the whole function, not only the pass.

quiz.why: No item is greater than the start value 0, so `best` never changes. Start from the first item instead.

takeaway: Set a start value, update it each pass, return it after the loop.

starters: Why must the accumulator be declared before the loop?
How do I find out why my loop returns the wrong total?
When should I choose for...of instead of a for loop?
